speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Since then, there have been profound changes in the data landscape, most notably in the sheer variety and volume of data that is being generated and its economic significance.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The typology of data is diverse – ranging from personal and machine-generated to meta data – with different risk implications.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The volume of data is growing at an unprecedented rate.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, Tera/Peta/Zetta bytes of data – you can pick your prefix – are being generated by ubiquitous Internet-of-Things or IoT devices and sensors, our real and virtual world activities, and smart machines in manufacturing and supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Data is also a key economic asset in the digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Data analytics provides valuable insights that inform decisions, generate efficiencies, enhance products and services, and power innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is a critical resource for emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, which hold much transformative potential.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our regulatory architecture must evolve and keep pace with these magnitudinal shifts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, we have initiated digital economy Agreements to position Singapore as a key node in the global network of digital flows and transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The proposed amendments to the PDPA are another step to ensure our legislative and regulatory regime is fit for purpose for a digital economy with a complex data landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our digital economy must be built on a solid foundation of trust.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Consumers must have the confidence that their personal data will be secure and used responsibly, even as they benefit from digital opportunities and data-driven services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Organisations need certainty to harness personal data for legitimate business purposes, with the requisite safeguards and accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The proposed amendments to the PDPA seek to strike this balance so as to maximise the potential benefits and minimise the risks of collecting and using personal data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In drafting the Bill, we have studied the data protection practices in jurisdictions like Australia, Canada, the European Union, Hong Kong and New Zealand.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The proposed amendments also incorporate valuable feedback received through four public consultation exercises.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, this principle of accountability is implied in sections 11 and 12 of the PDPA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill inserts a specific reference to accountability at Part III to make the principle explicit and to underscore its centrality.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This shift towards an accountability approach is in line with international trends and best practices in data protection laws.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It supports interoperability, allowing multi-national corporations to more easily adapt global best practices in Singapore, and minimises compliance costs for Singapore-based companies which are expanding globally.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In addition, organisations must notify both the PDPC and affected individuals when data breaches result, or are likely to result, in significant harm to individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This places the onus on organisations to assess the scale and impact of data breaches, ensures they are duly accountable to individuals for the personal data in their care, and empowers individuals to take timely measures to protect themselves if a data breach occurs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, clause 3 removes the current exclusion for agents of Government, thereby making clear that all private sector organisations are subject to the PDPA, even when they are acting on behalf of public agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, the Bill strengthens individual accountability for the egregious mishandling of data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Related amendments will also be made to the Public Sector (Governance) Act and the Monetary Authority of Singapore Act to align the public and private sector data regimes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: While the primary responsibility and liability for breaches of the PDPA rest with organisations, these new offences are aimed at individuals who know that their actions are not authorised or who act recklessly.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The clause provides for defences to the new offences, such as independent testing of anonymisation deployed in information security systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Also, these offences should not apply in situations where the conduct is solely in the nature of a private dispute, which should continue to be resolved through civil suits or other forms of dispute resolution.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 23 introduces section 48L, a statutory scheme under which the PDPC may, in lieu of a full investigation, accept written voluntary undertakings from organisations to remedy breaches and prevent their recurrence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, such undertakings may be accepted when organisations with effective monitoring and breach management systems notify the PDPC of a data breach, and undertake in writing to implement their breach management plan.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Several jurisdictions, like Australia, Canada and the UK, accept voluntary undertakings as part of their enforcement regimes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The PDPC will exercise this option only if it assesses that it will achieve an outcome similar or superior to a full investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For transparency, the undertakings, as well as the PDPC’s decisions and considerations for accepting them, will be made public.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the event of non-compliance, the PDPC may issue a direction requiring the organisation to comply with its undertakings, or initiate investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Section 48G of clause 23 empowers the PDPC to establish dispute resolution schemes for the resolution of customer complaints.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The PDPC may also direct complainants and organisations to attempt to resolve disputes via mediation, without the need to secure the consent of both parties.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 37 empowers the PDPC to require the attendance of an individual or employee to give statements and produce documents that are relevant to its investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This penalty framework is similar to that in other domestic regulation and legislation, including the Competition Act and the Telecommunications Act.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: During public consultations, concerns were raised about the higher financial penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 23 sets out amendments providing for the enforcement of the Do Not Call or DNC provisions under the same civil administrative regime as the data protection provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The new Part IXA of clause 22 also prohibits the use of dictionary attacks and address-harvesting software when sending messages to telephone numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The new section 48O under clause 23 of the Bill updates the current right of private action by a person who suffers loss or damage directly as a result of a breach of the data protection provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The right of private action will be extended to organisations and public agencies that suffer direct loss or damage arising from contraventions of the new business-to-business obligations in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Under the PDPA, individuals have the right to access their personal data, and request for corrections to be made or a copy to be provided.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Data portability is expected to spur competition and benefit consumers by encouraging the development of substitute as well as novel services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The PDPC will therefore work closely with all stakeholders for a phased implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Regulations will be issued in the coming months on the categories of data that should be portable and other technical and consumer protection details.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clauses 22 and 41 update both the PDPA and the Spam Control Act to rationalise and harmonise the requirements across all modern digital channels for direct commercial communication with consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The options for direct communications have evolved since the enactment of the PDPA’s DNC provisions and the Spam Control Act’s spam control provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, instant messaging on mobile devices has become the communication channel of choice for many consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With the proposed amendments, organisations can offer consumers a unified experience in managing their subscription to commercial communications.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Bill also recognises the development of an industry of third party DNC checkers, and delineates the responsibilities and obligations of DNC checkers and the organisations that commission them.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Currently, the PDPA recognises organisations’ need to use personal data for legitimate purposes, and accommodates them through exceptions to the consent requirement, or as deemed consent.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For all other purposes, organisations have to obtain consent from the individual.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The proposed amendments update, restructure and clarify the lawful purposes recognised as exceptions under the PDPA, and the deemed consent provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Multiple layers of contracting and outsourcing are common in modern commercial arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 6 therefore expands deemed consent to cater for scenarios where personal data is passed from an organisation to successive layers of contractors for the organisation to fulfil the contract with its customer.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Crucially, organisations relying on deemed consent for contractual necessity can only collect, use and disclose personal data where it is reasonably necessary to fulfil the contract with the individual.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clause 31 introduces the First Schedule to the PDPA, which sets out a new exception to consent for these legitimate uses of personal data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To rely on this exception, organisations must conduct an assessment to eliminate or reduce risks associated with the collection, use or disclosure of personal data, and must be satisfied that the overall benefit of doing so outweighs any residual adverse effect on an individual.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To ensure transparency, organisations must disclose when they rely on this exception.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: One of many potential use cases is anomaly detection in payment systems to prevent fraud or money-laundering.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The next set of enhancements supports innovation and introduction of new services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As a safeguard, this exception can be relied upon only for purposes that a reasonable person may consider appropriate in the circumstances and where the purpose cannot be achieved without the use of the personal data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Businesses have asked for this exception to also apply to entities within a group as they may consolidate corporate or administrative functions, or concentrate research and development expertise in a single unit that supports the entire group.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Bill provides for additional safeguards for intra-group sharing by requiring related corporations to be bound by a contract, agreement or binding corporate rules to implement and maintain appropriate safeguards for the personal data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The current research exception has also been revised in clause 32 to support commercial research and development that is not immediately directed at productisation, in other words, going upstream.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This could apply to research institutes carrying out scientific research and development, educational institutes embarking on social sciences research, and organisations conducting market research to identify and understand potential customer segments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Before doing so, organisations must conduct a risk assessment and conclude that the collection, use or disclosure of personal data in this manner will not likely have an adverse effect on the individual.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To illustrate, this would be useful for organisations that wish to use the personal data of existing customers for new purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, a financial institution may want to use voice data as an alternative means to authenticate and verify its customers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With these amendments, the financial institution can notify its customers of the intended use of their voice data, provide a reasonable opt-out period, and a contact number for customers’ queries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It should be noted that the individual may still withdraw his deemed consent any time after the opt-out period has lapsed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The PDPC will put in place safeguards to ensure that organisations work with anonymised data as much as possible, clearly assess and address any potential adverse effects on individuals, and continue to seek express consent for sending direct marketing messages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Fourth Industrial Revolution has perhaps already induced the fifth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is also set on this path as we strive towards becoming a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The risk of winner takes all is there and if this happens, where does that leave us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, there is urgency for us to transform and the urgency for us to transform is also increasing, in large part due to the on-going COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A consequence of digitalisation is that firms and people become more connected globally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This interconnectedness means access to bigger markets, which can be a boon for our talents and firms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is thankfully at the forefront in Asia for having the right conditions to embrace a digital economy and smart nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Against this background, we can understand the explosion of data in Singapore and the importance of data to our digital economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Intuitively, data for innovation and data protection seem to conflict with each other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need data to create and optimise products, processes and business models.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, there must be sufficient room for harnessing and using data.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Too much controls leads to high compliance costs and distracts firms from innovating.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, data protection, specifically personal data, is essential to protecting the privacy and interests of our citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Prior to the introduction of PDPA in 2012, public awareness of personal data protection was generally lower.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Anecdotally, we can easily recall instances in which people trustingly and freely share NRIC numbers and other personal information with various parties for various purposes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Consequently, besides receiving unwanted marketing material, they also become vulnerable to scams and crimes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having laws and a mechanism to sufficiently protect personal data engenders greater trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A clearly defined framework and laws that are effectively enforced will build consumers' confidence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One study of GDPR on how data protection regulation affects start-up innovation, published in November 2019, suggests that while the regulation appears to obstruct certain business models and technologies, it also clearly stimulated a certain amount of innovation and market opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More studies may be needed to study the effects of regulation on innovation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we can agree that data protection regulation builds trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A healthy dose of trust enables meaningful data to be shared and drives innovation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, a balanced approach to regulation is important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Facilitating the use of data in a way that does not erode consumer trust will enable Singapore to innovate better and faster, and stay competitive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, firms are no longer confined to Singapore with growing global connections.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They can operate out of Singapore and still access markets around the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the rise of cross-border e-trade and e-commerce, putting in place the right data laws will enhance our interoperability with global frameworks, thereby making it easier to do business and allow cross-border data flow.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A balance in this approach is hard to strike and I do note that four consultations had been conducted to date and I believe that this effort is to precisely to try to strike this balance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I do have four key concerns and would like to seek the Minister's clarifications.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, the introduction of data portability and extension of spam controls and DNC provisions to all direct communication platforms would give consumers more control over their own data.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But contraventions will now be dealt with as a civil proceeding in Court.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that this was originally a criminal proceeding.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My concern is that this perceived "step down" will diminish the importance of personal data protection and the severity of breaching the law.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can the Minister explain the rationale for this change?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, the deemed consent will now be enabled in this amendment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I understand this to be a move to avoid unnecessary inefficiencies in contracts with multiple layers of outsourcing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I am also concerned, whether this will weaken consumer protection and therefore again, consumer trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I note the measure that are put in place in Minister's speech earlier, I am just wondering what kind of risk-assessment and disclosure are we talking about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Would the Ministry regularly review whether these mechanisms are sufficient in providing sufficient protection and control to the consumers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, sufficient flexibility in harnessing and using data is needed for innovation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But many actions can be categorically explained as addressing one of such purposes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How will the Government prevent abuse in a more upstream manner?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government, as a body with regulatory powers and control over significant resources, will have to exercise greater discipline, caution and demonstrate transparency when handling personal data.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A better understanding of how the Government handles personal data will no doubt strengthen public trust.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Eight years is a long time in the digital age.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Technology has advanced by leaps and bounds and such technological improvements have also significantly changed our lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has one of the highest Internet penetration rates in the world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Eighty-eight percent of the population are Internet users and spend close to seven hours a day on the Internet on average.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They 8.9 million mobile connections, approximately 1.5 times more than the country's population.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The easy access of the Internet allows people to engage in content sharing, online shopping, access gaming sites and social media platforms amongst others.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The law, too, has to keep up with the times.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With increasing usage of such digital platforms comes increasing risk of personal data breaches.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Personal data such as names, phone numbers, emails and physical mailing addresses were being sold online.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate the effort to enhance the legal framework for the collection, use and disclosure of personal data, and to strengthen the accountability of organisations in respect of handling these data, I believe that there is still room for further refinement, namely in strengthening protection against unsolicited communication, clarifications on deemed consent and individuals rights under data portability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of such safeguards is the Do Not Call Registry when an individual can opt to be excluded for marketing or promotional messages.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, even with such safeguards in place, most Singaporeans still get unsolicited calls and messages from telesales agencies, moneylenders, illegal gambling advertisements and even phishing scam calls claiming to be from SingPost or DHL, asking them to collect the parcel.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Improved controls for unsolicited commercial messages and the section 43, would thus, be welcomed by consumers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A few years ago, I have personally lodged a Police report over persistent and unlicensed moneylending messages, but I was subsequently told by the Investigation Officer that the perpetrators are based overseas and that there is not much that we can do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledged that some of these calls and messages are from overseas or even from masked numbers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In particular, how does the Commission intend to take action against parties that are not even based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second is the topic on deemed consent and deemed consent by notification.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this makes sense, we should question if there are any mitigating factors to prevent the unwanted spreading of personal particulars or information from the third party organisation to subsequent parties for their benefit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, targeted marketing strategies as well as also raising the possible issue of increased risk of the spread of personal information.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With personal data held by multiple parties across multiple jurisdictions potentially, the risk of the data leak is much higher and data protection is only as strong as the weakest link.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, in the newly added section 15(a), deemed consent by notification, organisations are now able to collect information on the individual as long as the organisation has taken reasonable steps to inform the individual the organisation's intent, purpose to collect, use or disclose the person's data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The organisation itself also has to make sure that this is not likely to have an adverse effect on the individual.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Individuals also have the right to opt out or withdraw consent within a reasonable period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Section 15(a) also gives organisations the freedom to determine whether or not there is any adverse effect on the individual, which may not always be interpreted in the individual's favour.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The new provision does serve as an exception to the consent obligation and moves the data protection framework away from express and explicit consent to implicit consent from individuals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, online shopping algorithms are designed to identify the type of product a person is interested in and to suggest to the person, items that he or she may like to purchase.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If a person for example, has conditions that decreases his overall well-being with these advertisements, for example, having compulsive buying disorder, is that deemed as an adverse effect that should be intervened?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An organisation needs to identify and implement reasonable measures to eliminate or reduce the probability of the adverse effect.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What are some of the ways that these can be executed in reality?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, what is regarded as a reasonable period for individuals to opt out?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are businesses allowed to determine this or will the commission be providing some guidance on the general timeframe?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The PDPC could consider something similar by carving out exceptional categories of data where deemed consent by notification, cannot work or requires express consent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, on the new Part VIB on data portability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This may pose issues for individuals that may want to limit or select the data they would like to hand over to the receiving organisation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And this will be unlike Article 20 of the European GDPR, which gives individuals the right to receive the personal data concerning him or her.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that there is an "access request" under section 21 of the current PDPA, where individuals may be able to get a copy of their personal data that is under the possession of the originating organisation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, it is unclear to what extent this will apply hand-in-hand with the data portability obligation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further in this digital world, it is often been said that, "the Internet never forgets".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would then truly give meaning to the phrase under section 26G and that is to provide individuals with greater autonomy and control over their personal data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What has perhaps not been fully addressed is firstly, the ability to enforce such rules to protect against unsolicited messages, particularly from overseas parties; secondly, the power imbalance between organisations and individuals under a deemed consent opt-out regime; and finally, the individual’s rights to his or her data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this rapidly evolving digital age, it is imperative that we constantly assess and fine-tune the PDPA, in order to maintain the effectiveness of its safeguards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, it has become even more important for us to ensure that our data protection legislation is keeping pace with advances in information technology.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that users were informed quite quickly and were thus able to take measures to protect themselves, such as changing their passwords.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will compel all companies to step up controls or risk heavy financial penalties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I note that notifications are only required where there are significant number of people affected, which had previously been proposed at 500 or more, and where there could be significant harm for affected individuals, such as compromised NRIC and credit card numbers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would therefore like to ask the Minister why notifications to PDPC need be made only when the breaches involve a prescribed number of people?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I feel that as long as an individual is affected, PDPC should be informed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that the current online reporting form for data breaches is already quite a simple one-page form that takes about eight to 10 minutes to fill up, and hence reporting should not be too onerous for organisations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, any individual acting in a personal or domestic basis will not be caught by these obligations, as such a case is already excluded from the Act.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This in effect means that there is no timeframe set for notifying individuals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I feel that there should be a clear deadline so that individuals can do the needful to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The longer it takes to inform them, the greater the potential damage, and the PDPA is not simply a notification regime, but is also an Act that protects individuals and their data.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Individuals may also need to take their own steps to change, mask or protect their data, including those on other platforms, especially if the leaks involve their digital identities, which are increasingly interlinked.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   In addition, the Bill specified that PDPC must be notified within 72 hours, and affected persons, without undue delay.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This in effect, means that there is no timeframe set for notifying individuals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I feel that there should be a clear deadline so that individuals can do the needful to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The longer it takes to inform them, the greater the potential damage, and the PDPA is not simply a notification regime, but is also an Act that protects individuals and their data.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Individuals may also need to take their own steps to change, mask or protect their data, including those on other platforms, especially if the leaks involve their digital identities, which are increasingly interlinked.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): I welcome more stringent controls over spam and telemarketing through related amendments to the Spam Control Act or SCA.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The most common messages make offers of loans, gambling and betting.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My question is how the Ministry would deal with perpetrators from overseas.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can they be caught and what recourse do our people have, besides blocking these numbers as and when they attack?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry be able to explore cross-jurisdictional cooperation with countries where these overseas numbers have originated from, so that there is a possibility of either bringing these syndicates to justice or at least to shut them down?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If there are gaps, would PDPC consider providing more resources and experts at a reasonable or low cost to help and guide these companies, since prevention is always better than cure?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Cross-border data flows and data capitalisation is increasing the importance for business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The current regime of consent-based data protection faces challenges from the rapid, technological developments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In addition, the recent data breaches suffered by the likes of Lazada, Razer and Eatigo evidenced the need for solid personal data protection laws.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Personal data protection laws must offer adequate protection to individuals but still allow businesses to remain agile and competitive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These amendments should attend to a basic tenet of protecting the rights of individuals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This concept may be ambiguous in certain contexts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Without further guidance on the scope of legitimate interests, especially for vulnerable segments such as children be provided.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This will ensure that individuals are protected and companies can comply to requirements efficiently and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The concept of significant harm and significant scale may again ne very ambiguous.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, would further guidance of the concept of significant harm and significant scale be provided.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I agree with the need to strengthen the accountability of organisations and enabling of meaningful consent as reflected in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The protection of personal data is a concern of all Singaporeans, particularly when they learn about mass data breaches suffered by public agencies and private companies, both here and abroad.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is now greater public awareness among members of the public and organisations of the need to safeguard personal data.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The public has a right to demand strong protection of their personal data.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, policy-makers have to be aware of the business costs of complying with stringent regulations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is thus necessary to make periodic amendments to the Personal Data Protection Act or PDPA and the Spam Control Act to bring our data privacy regulations more in line with current realities and global norms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will focus on three areas in my speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, ensuring that personal data is protected where it matters to citizens, yet without unnecessarily burdening business with regulations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, aligning the PDPA with the GDPR, the European Union's general data protection regulation to avoid conflating rules.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, harmonising the Government's data protection rules with the PDPA to ensure that Government agencies safeguard personal data the same way as it expects private sector companies to do.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Everyone wants their personal data protected from prying eyes and unwanted marketers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No one likes being interrupted by unsolicited phone calls from people they do not know, trying to sell things that they do not want or tricking them into sharing confidential information.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They certainly do not want scammers using their NRIC address or credit card numbers to take up unauthorised loans, buy stolen goods or, worst of all, sell their personal data on the dark web.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We had made good progress in personal data protection since the introduction of the PDPA in 2012.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, despite being on the Do Not Call Registry since 2013, I still get phone calls or text messages from individuals offering cheap loans, access to illegal gambling sites or asking me to pick up packages which I never ordered.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have met residents who were scammed of tens of thousands of dollars by swindlers who persuaded them over the phone to reveal their Internet banking passwords or one-time PINs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Still others had loans in their names taken up with loan sharks because their NRICs were misused.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For most Singaporeans, these are the biggest concerns with regard to personal data privacy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, fewer people are concerned about what kind of cookies a website is using to track them and many find cookie notices on websites nowadays more of an irritant than a privacy protecting measure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is a debate going on about how to stop big tech companies from hoovering our personal data in order to serve us tailored advertisements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a valid concern but not something that keeps the average citizen awake at night.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Privacy regulations should therefore give greater focus to the areas of data privacy that matter most to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will now move on to discussing the PDPA and GDPR.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The general data protection regulation is a wide-ranging personal data protection legislation from the EU which has extraterritorial effect.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The GDPR applies not only to European companies but also to Singapore companies that offer goods and services to individuals in the EU, even if those companies do not have an EU presence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, the GDPR provides extra protection for special categories of data, which include data about an individual's race, religion, political opinions and health information.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The PDPA does not specifically define what constitutes sensitive personal data although guidance from PDPC suggests that personal data of a sensitive nature should be accorded a higher level of protection as a matter of good practice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The GDPR also sets a more stringent standard for consent, which must be obtained in a clear, open, specific and transparent manner.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Despite its less prescriptive approach compared to the GDPR, the PDPA's model may be preferred by countries whose approach towards privacy is closer to Singapore's than the EU's.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we should guard against the PDPA acquiring a reputation of providing a GDPR-minus standard of personal data protection.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It would be much better if the PDPA were known internationally as a law that strikes the right balance between data protection and business efficiency.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the PDPA may not be identical to the GDPR, it should not have provisions or interpretations which are in conflict with the GDPR.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This way, Singapore businesses, which need to comply with the GDPR will be able to rest easy, knowing that they also comply with the PDPA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on my analysis of the PDPA, I am glad to note that this currently appears to be the case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope that this approach will continue through future amendments to the PDPA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My last point concerns the personal data protection obligations of the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have worked with the Government both as a civil servant and a government contractor, and I am well aware of the robust rules and practices in place to safeguard personal data.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, complying with a different set of data protection rules from the private sector is problematic for several reasons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the data protection provisions in the various Acts differ in their standard of protection.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is not surprising since these laws were enacted long before the PDPA and without the specific purpose of general data protection in mind.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Having public data controllers governed by a hodge podge of separate legislation is likely to lead to differing standards and gaps in coverage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, the lack of a single set of rules governing privacy leaves individual data owners unclear as to what level of personal data protection they are entitled to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most individuals concerned about privacy would be more familiar with the protections provided under the PDPA than what is provided for under the PSGA, OSA, ITA, IM8 and others.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the IM8 is not even a public document that ordinary citizens can access.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government's exemption from the PDPA could lead to concerns among citizens about how their sensitive data is being used by the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, many are now worried about how the information collected by SafeEntry and Trace Together will be processed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others continue to worry about how our security services may be collecting and sharing sensitive information about citizens with little independent oversight.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, the Government regulations cover mainly internal checks on the Government Ministries and agencies, and criminal and disciplinary consequences for individual officers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could be seen as a lower threshold of accountability on the part of the Government should data beaches occur.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why should public data controllers be treated differently from private data controllers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe there is merit in having a universal standard of personal data protection that applies to both private as well as public data controllers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can be achieved without causing undue inefficiencies in the functioning of businesses or the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to continue to update the PDPA to keep up with the realities on the ground.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government should hold itself to the same level of data privacy standards, procedures and accountability it expects of private sector companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Against this backdrop, the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This looks to ensuring the protection and responsible use of personal data by organisations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clear accountability on what data is collected, used and disclosed digitally or even physically, will help in building consumers' trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For businesses, having clarity on the use of personal data and the trust of consumers will give them the confidence to use the data to innovate and improve services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With advancement in technology, the volume of personal data collected and aggregated is vast and growing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With capabilities like data analytics, machine learning and artificial intelligence making sense of the data and using it to gain valuable insights is real.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If used appropriately, this can provide benefits but it can also be exploited for not so well-meaning purposes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To strengthen trust and at the same time derive the value of data, we need to balance and handle the "right to data privacy", "data security" and "the proper use of data to innovate".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My speech will focus on trust which I believe is core to achieving the objectives of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will speak on two aspects of the proposed amendment which are key to protecting data while appropriately enabling the leverage of data for innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will enchance the protection for indivduals and is key to building trust with individuals on how their personal data is used.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Second, amendment of section 15 regarding "deemed consent" and changes to the exceptions and the new section 15A "deemed consent by notification" and a reasonable period and manner for the individual to withdraw consent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Cybercrime statistics show that data breaches continue to rise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And just to cite one example, on SafeatLast Editor's Choice, one of the key cybercrime statistics, that a hacker attack takes place every 39 seconds.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, you can imagine, as I am speaking here, by the time I finish my speech, the number of attacks that have happened.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, notification to individuals is important because it will allow them to take timely mitigating measures but also it is important that there is notification because it allows the national actions, both of the organisations and other organisations impacted to take the necessary actions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With increased accountability, offences and penalties – while I do agree that it is necessary – there may also be a danger of organisations becoming overly risk averse to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This seems a little strange but one would say it is okay for organisations to protect themselves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If they do all the right things, individuals will be protected.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If the scale is on organisations protecting themselves from being penalised or against enforcement, we may also lose the focus on actually protecting consumer's data privacy and risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may also have a negative impact on the desire to use data appropriately to innovate and improve productivity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill's introduction to require organisations to conduct risk assessments to identify and mitigate the adverse impact on individuals is the right approach because it balances this, because it allows organisations to analyse what is the real risk and really then make that decision of being able to notify and then decide to innovate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will later touch on this in my speech on the point about "deemed consent" associated with the risk assessments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These amendments to strengthen accountability of organisations are necessary as they give businesses clear guidelines on how they handle personal data.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must, however, recognise that there will be compliance costs associated.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given the value of personal data and the inherent risks, I think it is important that organisations take the responsibility and it is a necessary cost of doing business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But with the current economic challenges, can the Minister also share if there will be any support given to businesses in managing the increased cost of compliance and also the increased complexity of compliance?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As businesses may need to partner, subcontract and outsource services to deliver their contractual obligations to customers, the amendments proposed for section 15 introduces deemed consent by contractual necessity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think this is important because it does recognise a new business model and facilitates collection, use and disclosure of personal data by organisations with their contractors and partners to enable better understanding of customers for more effective performance and fulfillment of contractual obligations to customers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But let me now touch on the introduction of the new section 15A relating to deemed consent by notification.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will allow them to collect and process personal data to use, to improves services as well as productivity research purposes and also for fraud detection and security.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The requirements outlined in the Bill for notification, the manner and the period for individuals to opt out are fairly broad.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because many of us today, we just tick that box that says "I consent" but not realising that actually, even when you do not do it, it is deemed consent and therefore it is an uninformed consent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And if consumers understand that fundamentally, then the protection and the appropriate use of information will be there because organisations will have that confidence to use the data.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But having worked through the details of the Bill, and I must admit that there was quite a lot of details on the Bill, I see that it does strive to achieve the difficult balance of protecting consumer personal data and, at the same time, not limit the use of data to innovate and deliver greater benefit.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In today's day and age and the role that Singapore plays, I think it is important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do want to make a special mention to the team that worked on this because, clearly there was a lot of work put in and a lot of thought given in terms of that balance because when I first started looking at this amendment Bill, I actually had the very opposite feeling about it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But having gone through the details, I think there has been very good thought given to strengthening of accountability but at the same time, not limiting that use of data for innovations while protecting individuals' privacy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that success will be achieved when individuals trust that their personal data is protected.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this will in turn gives organisations confidence to use and leverage the data for insights to deliver value.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not oppose the Bill and agree with the comments expressed by my Parliamentary colleagues Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Louis Chua Kheng Wee.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other words, it would be helpful if the Government could provide a statutory definition or further guidance as to the factors that are to be taken into account in assessing the nature of the "harm" and any relevant thresholds before the PDPC would hold the view that "significant harm" has been occasioned, so that organisations have clarity in their assessment as to when a data breach will be considered a notifiable data breach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this clause, the obligation to notify affected individuals can be waived "subject to any conditions that the   thinks fit".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given that such an overly broad "escape" clause may undermine the legal spirit of the mandatory data breach notification requirement, I would like to ask: what are circumstances in which the Government may activate this clause, and would the Government consider tightening and carefully circumscribing the scope and use of this clause, to reduce any potential for abuse and the perception of arbitrariness?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The thrust of the PDPA is to hold businesses responsible such that risk can be treated as a business cost rather than something to be potentially placed on individual "scapegoats" who may have little bargaining power as employees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Junior employees with lesser bargaining power may be held liable, while higher ranked employees and the organisation itself may face reduced accountability thereby.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While the amendments spell out possible grounds of defence that the accused individual may take, has the Government given some thought to what additional measures should be put in place to prevent such "scapegoating"?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, businesses, especially SMEs, sole proprietorships and some not-for-profit organisations, may experience difficulties in adhering to these new, more rigorous regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a suggestion would be in line with, firstly, the previous 18-month transition period adopted before most of the substantive provisions of the PDPA took effect when it was enacted in 2012; and secondly, the two-year transition or sunrise period which was given when the GDPR was adopted by the European Union in 2016, during which	time there was delayed enforcement so that organisations would have time to prepare.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: During this transition period, the PDPC could consider providing greater support to SMEs and volunteer organisations in several respects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in the 2018 SingHealth data breach, the delay of 28 days in the reporting of the incident to senior management could be attributed to lack of staff training and absence of a reporting framework to some extent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Voluntary organisations, in particular, may benefit from such training as they may lack knowledge of these requirements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in 2019, Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association was found by the PDPC to have been negligent in failing to make reasonable security arrangements to protect members' personal data and appoint a Data Protection Officer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would be particularly helpful for SMEs and business-to-business or B2B companies in Singapore, as these often store data in an unstructured way, using folders in an ad hoc fashion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As such, if a data breach were to happen, the data review process could be particularly complex, time-consuming and costly for them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I rise in support of this Bill, which seeks to achieve the twin objectives of strengthening consumer confidence that their personal data will be used responsibly; and enabling organisations to confidently harness personal data for innovation which, in turn, would benefit our citizens and Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It has been eight years since the PDPA was enacted in 2012.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Undeniably, there will be some who will question the timing and impact of these proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: After all, we are only starting to see the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic unravelling and facing a probable imminent global recession.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These amendments will necessitate changes in an organisation’s policies, systems and processes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With organisations already trying to cope with stretched resources and trying to avoid going belly-up, measures, such as stiffer fines for data breaches or making it mandatory for organisations to notify the PDPC, may seem counterproductive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Nevertheless, I support the proposed amendments for the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These long-contemplated amendments are vital and tabled none too soon.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we have read in the news, e-commerce and tech companies are looking to expand or invest in Singapore, using Singapore as a launchpad for expansion, not only into the ASEAN region but globally as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore has hereinafter taken steps to establish and position itself as a data hub.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is, therefore, no better time than the present to refine our data protection regulations as we continue in our race to lead in a data-driven economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must recognise and seize these opportunities to ride the tech wave.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Speaking also as the Assistant Secretary-General of NTUC, the creation of job opportunities and the sharpening of Singapore’s innovation capability, without question, would, and can only, be advantageous to our workers in this current economic climate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The refinement of our data protection framework and policies that support the growth of our digital economy is an essential element in our nation's overall blueprint for the future and for continued growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With our infrastructure and links to the region and the world, we are in a good position to ride the tech wave and to continue tapping and building on our potential and strengths.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Furthermore, data protection laws are still in an early evolutionary stage globally.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These proposed amendments seek to bring our data protection laws in greater alignment with the global standard.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, our aspiration is not just to keep up with the data protection regulations like the GDPR.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have more than a fighting chance of becoming one of the leading authorities in data protection in the region and in the world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, consumers are increasingly aware and concerned about the way their personal data is being collected, used and shared.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They demand for convenience, speed, personalised user experience, flexibility and, at the same time, greater confidence and assurance in the way their personal data is safeguarded and used.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Where consent is not sought, safeguards will be put in place for organisations to be held accountable for their practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, with the introduction of the notification with opt-out option, organisations will be able to obtain meaningful consent from consumers and use this data in new ways.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, organisations must first ascertain that there is no adverse effect on the individual before obtaining consent in this manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even as businesses are given more scope to leverage data, consumers will still have flexibility and the ability to opt out if and when they so choose.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For businesses concerned with the increase in the limits of financial penalties, I think there is no cause for alarm, as this is targeted towards irresponsible organisations in the most serious cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Similarly, the introduction of new offences is only intended for individuals who egregiously mishandle personal data and not where employees are acting within the scope of their employment, or for data professionals, cybersecurity specialists, artificial intelligence engineers or researchers carrying out legitimate activities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While I am supportive of the amendments to this Bill, I would be grateful if the Minister could address the following concerns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, the costs and investment in complying with the new data portability obligation may be significant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Will organisations, especially SMEs, receive any assistance in this regard?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can the Minister share how MCI or PDPC plans to help reduce the compliance burden on organisations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data protection has become only more concerning and this Bill helps address those concerns.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened by the amendments requiring organisations to inform people who are affected by data breaches and to help people port their data to other services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These changes will help Singaporeans feel a greater sense of control over their data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have three points of clarification on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the Commission intends to prescribe classes of personal data considered likely to result in significant harm to individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond this, can Minister clarify what other circumstances will be prescribed to help organisations assess whether a data breach may lead to “significant harm” to affected individuals under section 26B?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can Minister clarify what standard the Commission will apply when it reviews an organisation’s assessment on whether a data breach is notifiable?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An organisation may decide not to notify affected individuals of a data breach because they assess that there was no significant harm caused and the breach was not of a significant scale.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the Commissioner later disagrees with this assessment and reviews the organisation’s assessment, will the Commissioner do so by holding the organisation to the standard of a reasonable person?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister also clarify whether the Commission will consider a good-faith, systematic assessment by an organisation as a mitigating factor in deciding whether and how much to penalise the organisation for failing to notify the Commission of a data breach?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the definition of adverse effect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In several cases, they have to assess whether their action will have an “adverse effect” on individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 15A, organisations have to assess the extent of adverse effect to decide whether deemed consent by notification is sufficient consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 17, organisations have to weigh such adverse effects against the “legitimate interests” of the organisation or of other people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister define what it means to impose an “adverse effect” on an individual and what are some examples of it?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such clarity is important because organisations will likely face practical challenges in identifying every possible adverse effect on an individual, and a wrong assessment may lead to harsher penalties for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In line with the Act’s shift to a risk-based accountability approach, I would also suggest applying a standard of reasonableness when determining whether organisations have fulfilled their obligations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, they should be required to assess the “adverse effect” on an individual only to the standard of a reasonable person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will help organisations comply with the new Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about data porting obligation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill empowers individuals to make data porting requests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means individuals can ask organisations to send their personal information to other organisations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Organisations can say no only under conditions outlined in the new Twelfth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Commission be releasing guidelines and examples to help organisations understand whether each of the conditions applies to them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, these guidelines should clarify when the data would “reveal confidential commercial information” that could “harm the competitive position of the organisation”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure many companies will be keen to cite this condition if they are asked to transfer data to a competitor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the guidelines should clarify when the data is “trivial”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the guidelines should clarify when the data porting request is “frivolous” or “vexatious”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Data porting is a new concept to many organisations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Organisations will benefit from greater clarity on what counts as trivial, frivolous or vexatious.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill is a timely and necessary effort to strengthen personal data management.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The pandemic has accelerated the need to go digital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This results in the sharing of personal data with businesses in exchange for their products and services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And unless the data is carefully protected, it will expose many people vulnerable to cybercrimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: According to a July CNBC report, large-scale data breaches have grown in intensity and frequency in 2020.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is largely attributed to more businesses being conducted online during the COVID period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate the move to enhance the Do Not Call provisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The popularity of instant messaging platforms like Whatsapp, Telegram and WeChat has surpassed that of SMSes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During lockdowns, these are the platforms that residents use to communicate with each other, especially between seniors and their families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But many of these platforms have been abused to spread fake news, commit fraud and scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They can even spread malicious links containing malware.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We hear of scammers making phone calls supposedly representing MOH during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many seniors, including several from my constituency, have reported falling prey to scams and unsolicited advertisements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many of these fraudulent messages are from overseas sources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And some phone numbers have been spoofed to conceal the perpetrator’s actual number.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, it is impossible to report them to the authorities, or to block them on your handphone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If not, what can be done to safeguard the interests of phone users?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite success in the reduction of unsolicited marketing messages from commercial companies, users are at greater risk of more sinister problems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These include scams via robo-calls and text messages from unlicensed moneylenders and online gambling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She got a message from an overseas company offering her an investment proposal that promised her 20% annual returns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She did some simple checks on the company.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: After some brief interactions over email, she decided to wire across the money to the company.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She has not heard from the company since.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If someone like Mdm K can fall for such a scam, other residents like seniors are at an even higher risk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This case highlights that the Government today has no reach to those entities with criminal intent and especially those that originate overseas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, consumers will need to exercise caution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And this may be an area where technology can provide a solution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should encourage our entrepreneurs to think of similar solutions for phone and SMS apps.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many invested a large sum of money to pivot their businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For them, there is still a steep learning curve to scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They have to now deal with this new enhanced responsibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Undoubtedly this would be an added burden on their operations and finances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may then pass on the additional costs to the consumers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share how can Government help them to meet the new requirements without imposing too much on these businesses’ finances?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As regulations for companies to gain access and share data for innovation is relaxed, good data collection and protection practices will be increasingly pertinent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Big Data has been mostly lauded for its contribution to innovative product development and improved user experiences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica data scandal was a wake-up call.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, the Government must invest in creating a strong eco-system that protects our data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The efforts must be transparently communicated to consumers to retain their faith in the system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must be more discerning of the types of information that can be collected and shared, with or without consent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, it is a common marketing practice to entice consumers to sign up for a promotion or a freebie.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And consumers are required to mark a little box at the end of the form, giving consent to use the data for marketing purposes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is well and easy to say, if you don’t feel comfortable handing over your information, you don’t have to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: No one is forcing you to sign up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But these marketing techniques leverage a common human weakness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And this is the inclination to act on a good deal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And at that moment, sharing one’s personal information may seem of little consequence until a data breach happens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is therefore critical, as part of measures to enhance data protection, that we do more to prevent the indiscriminate collection of highly personal data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That said, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the use of consumer data to spur innovation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The development of more exciting, relevant products and services will open up new business opportunities and new markets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has also highlighted the critical need for digitalisation at the personal, as well as organisational level.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
