text: We have done well to keep abreast with this development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, if Singapore wants to keep its leading position in the international digital economy, we must recognise the key role that data privacy plays in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, knowingly or unknowingly, personal data is already being shared and traded.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When consumers share personal data, there must be robust safeguards to protect their privacy so that we can increase trust and level of participation by one and all in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must at the same time be mindful that as an innovation hub, businesses and organisations must be able to harness data confidently in their search for creative solutions and ways to improve consumers’ experiences, products and services.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In order to enhance the protection of consumer data, we must support increased accountability by organisations and businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There was no legal requirement or compulsion to inform the consumer of information breaches.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lazada has been forthcoming in this instance and had actively monitored their data security systems, while Eatigo was able to detect the breach after it’s users’ data was put on sale online.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This should convince us that we cannot leave consumer data security to chance, hoping that businesses and organisations will act in an ethical manner whenever information breaches happen.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This strengthens the confidence of consumers in the organisation’s ability to protect their privacy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Data portability would benefit both consumers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ease and security of data portability provides consumer autonomy over their personal data, and plausibly, increase the consumer participation rate in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, it can provide access to data for businesses to better serve their customers’ needs or to provide innovative solutions for their clients.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, how do we prevent companies from exploiting this ease of portability to manipulate customers and shape their behaviour?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we protect consumers from exploitative and manipulative marketing techniques once businesses get a hold of consumer data?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do less tech-savvy customers, such as our senior citizens and other vulnerable groups understand the implications when they consent to port their data over?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At which point does using portable data for highly personalised service becomes exploitation for profit-making purposes, especially if it is used to exploit an individual's pre-existing condition such as compulsive buying disorder?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What if a customer just wants part of his data to be ported?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are important questions we need to answer to assure the public that their privacy is protected.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To illustrate these concerns, take for example a vulnerable consumer giving consent or is perceived to have provided deemed consent to an e-commerce site to port his data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The e-commerce vendor proceeds to use it and may even proliferate the data indiscriminately, and he falls prey to questionable marketing techniques.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we protect the vulnerable who are less digitally savvy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think we can all agree that spam marketing messages in the form of voice calls, text and fax messages are a nuisance and not to mention highly intrusive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thus, I am supportive of such Do Not Call provisions or DNC under the PDPA.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, considering that the digital economy is global in nature and is not bounded by the jurisdiction of nation-state borders, how do we enforce these DNC provisions to overseas companies?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there even ways to minimise the ability of overseas businesses from spamming our consumers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Conversely, how do we ensure that Singapore registered businesses and organisations handle their data ethically when they port them over to overseas vendors and partners?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What safeguards do we have to ensure that the data is not proliferated and subsequently manipulated for commercial gains from overseas?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Increasingly, there is the necessity in providing disclosure of personal and even organisational data by a business to its partners or contractors in order to assess and review contractual performance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This may result in multiple layers of outsourcing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses and organisations can then use this disclosed data for their own purposes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, when businesses and organisations require such data, there should be pre-arranged stipulations such that there is either a time-bound or scope-bound condition in order for the disclosed data to not be traded or sold to other organisations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would go towards making data disclosure more secure and again, increase participation in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It also avoids the situation where disclosed data is knowingly or unknowingly used by other organisations for their own purposes other than that which was agreed upon by the initial contractual obligation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is a measure of increased protection for the consumers, as well as more punitive consequences for businesses and organisations who have not taken adequate safety precautions when using data that is made available to them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To enhance the amendments to the Bill further, I propose considering the following.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One, more must be done to educate the vulnerable so they are aware of what they are consenting to.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would help ensure that all are protected and not unfairly taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Two, guidelines are also to be drawn up to help ensure the ethical use of data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These guidelines should be based on ethical considerations and not on commercial or profit interests of businesses and organisations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Three, digital literacy programmes for youths should include the awareness of personal data protection, as well as ethical considerations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our youths are entering a world where the digital landscape is ever evolving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We will have to depend on them to define how data is being used ethically.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And finally, fifth in the absence of the possibility for enforcement, we need to explore ways to protect consumer data from being used or proliferated by foreign companies and businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   With this amendment, we are protecting consumer data security in addition to ensuring that businesses and organisations act more responsibly when using data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This amendment will hopefully increase consumer trust and level of participation in the ever-evolving digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are measures to increase protection for the consumers as well as more punitive consequences for businesses and organisations who have not taken adequate safety precautions when using the data that is made available to them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to suggest the following.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, we must enhance awareness and educate those who are less digitally capable within our community so that they can be aware of what they are consenting to.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will help ensure that they are protected against those who try to take advantage of them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, guidelines must also be drawn up to help ensure ethical use of data by businesses and organisations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, we also need to educate our youths with literacy programmes that include awareness of personal data protection as well as ethical considerations in a digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our youths are entering a world where the digital landscape is constantly evolving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have to depend on them to define how data is used ethically in the future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As consumers and business owners, we must bear the responsibility and further strengthen our understanding of data usage and data privacy, and we must continue to use data to drive innovation in order to transform our economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In summary, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, given that Singapore is at the forefront on data privacy laws especially in our immediate region, we need a level playing field between Singapore companies and foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot be overly restrictive but we must still do our utmost to protect our consumers from intrusive, manipulative and exploitative practices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to give consumers the choice and control over their personal data and how it is used.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, clarifications notwithstanding, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some would see this as a small amount for such a large company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to know if the PDPC intends to punish repeat offenders more severely, as repeated offences simply go to show that the organisation has not implemented the necessary safeguards to properly protect personal data, despite previous reported lapses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many residents have told me that they continue to receive spam calls and text messages related to online gambling and unlicensed moneylending, despite having registered their phone numbers in the Do-Not-Call or DNC registry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This makes them question what was the point of registering their numbers in the DNC registry in the first place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore support the proposed enhancements to the Spam Control Act 2007 and the DNC provisions, which will serve to provide consumers with more protection from unwanted communications across various platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite the enhancements, we need to recognise that many spam text messages and calls originate from scammers or unlicensed moneylenders based overseas.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Ministry could work with our telcos to explore the use of technology to prevent such unsolicited messages, which often contain malware links, as well as spam robo-calls.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the United States, their mobile and broadband providers have worked with the government to create a new protocol called STIR/SHAKEN, which provides a secure mechanism for service providers to cryptographically sign and verify the Caller ID for calls made over the Internet.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This has seemingly helped to combat Caller ID spoofing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Could the Ministry explore implementing similar technology here?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers need to be personal-data-literate and understand what they are consenting to when they tick off the checkboxes under a company's User Agreement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Often, many consumers do not fully read the terms and conditions, as they are written in small font sizes and clauses are often hidden behind many technical jargons.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Hence, many simply just check the accept button, not knowing that they would then unwittingly give up their personal data, sometimes in perpetuity, to these commercial entities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We therefore need to educate consumers about personal data literacy, even as the PDPC works to ensure that businesses safeguard data responsibly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to urge the PDPC to publish guidelines on how companies should highlight their key User Agreement terms and conditions in a simple and upfront manner, preferably in large font size, and make clear to consumers about the categories of personal data that these companies will collect and how they intend to use them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The proposed amendments to the PDPA are significant and it is likely that many organisations will incur additional costs in adapting to these new regulations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, companies will have to undertake an extensive review of their data protection procedures to ensure that they meet the Bill's expanded scope of "deemed consent", as well as ensure that their current systems are able to comply with the new data portability obligation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many businesses are already reeling from the impact of COVID-19 and they are worried about the cost of adhering to the revised regime.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I do think that we need to mete out more deterrent penalties to organisations that continually fail to safeguard the personal data of consumers, as having a stringent data protection policy is important to further strengthen Singapore's position as the region's leading data hub.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We also need to focus on educating Singaporeans about personal data literacy, as more organisations seek to collect and monetise our personal data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Personal data protection is essential for today's increasingly data-driven economy to function effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without adequate safeguards regulating the usage and protection of data, consumers' confidence can be eroded, making it difficult for legitimate companies and entities to operate optimally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The amendments bring Singapore's data protection regime a step closer to the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation or GDPR.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter has been internationally regarded as the gold standard for the protection of consumer data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the expanded responsibility of organisations under the amendments, I am glad to know that many of the businesses consulted welcome the amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This demonstrates their cognisance of the value of a robust data privacy regime, especially with the rise of malicious cyber-actors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that the amendments have tried to carefully balance the interests of both consumers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Individuals will have greater control over their data with, for example, the new data portability obligation and the tighter rules on telemarketing with the enhanced DNC provisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, the strengthened penalty regime under the amendments will drive an appropriate investment by companies into data protection and compliance efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, sufficient flexibility is provided through the exceptions to consent provisions to meet commercial needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Per Part 3, section 1(2)(a), the legitimate interest is viewed from an organisation's perspective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This inadvertently encompasses a subjective determination on the part of the organisation in assessing whether their legitimate interests outweigh potential adverse effects on an individual.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While section 2 to 10 provides some circumstances whereby the collection, use or disclosure of personal data is necessary, these circumstances may be limited in scope, except for section 2 where the meaning of "evaluative purposes" is seemingly ambiguous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As such, I seek the Ministry's direction to provide guidance on what constitutes "evaluative purposes".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, to minimise disputes, perhaps the Ministry may consider looking into prescribing broader, objective guidelines on what constitutes legitimate interests to firstly, ensure greater ease of compliance for organisations who seek to rely on this exception and secondly, enhance consumers' understanding of their rights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, considering that the collection, usage and disclosure of personal data are central to the business models of data collection and survey companies, I would like to clarify with the Ministry if the availability of this exception should similarly apply to such companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My second clarification relates to the new Data Portability Obligation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a important advancement in Singapore's data privacy regime, allowing individuals to regain more control over their data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, my concern with this obligation lies within its potential impact on businesses costs and operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some businesses consulted have cited significant compliance costs, efforts and manpower requirements in meeting these new regulations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This includes tailoring current processes for larger businesses and the construction of new technological structures for smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the global economy experiencing a hard hit from the COVID-19 pandemic, many SMEs are already struggling to stay afloat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In light of this, I have three suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would help businesses to tide through the COVID-19 crisis and provide an appropriate duration of time to comply with this new obligation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Government support SMEs in setting up basic technological structures to do so?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps the Government can work with unions and trade associations or TACs, for these support platforms to help smaller businesses comply with the new obligations imposed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The unions and TACs can also update businesses, train them, especially SMEs, on the revised amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC’s Learning Hub currently conducts data-protection related courses and the scope of courses can be expanded to complement the amendments made to the Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, section 26H affords consumers the avenue to apply to the Commission to review a porting organisation’s failure to transmit the applicable data within a reasonable period of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Instead of a subjective measure of time, could the Ministry prescribe a stipulated duration of time to fulfil the porting request, with the subjectively determined "reasonable time" only applying in situations where businesses require more than the stipulated time to do so?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would better help businesses and consumers manage their duties and expectations respectively, reducing unmeritorious complaints to the Commission.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My third point of clarification relates to the increased financial penalties under the amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the penalty imposed on a contravening organisation will vary naturally according to the facts, this might artificially create the impression that the financial penalties under Singapore’s data privacy regime are much harsher compared to those of its neighbours.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The right to erasure is recognised in other jurisdictions, such as the EU’s GDPR.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Article 17 of the GDPR affords individuals the right to obtain from data controllers the erasure of personal data and the obligation on controllers to erase the concerned data without undue delay under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, where the personal data is no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Similarly, under section 25 of the PDPA, the retention limit obligation is imposed on organisations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under this, organisations shall cease to retain personal data where the purpose for which that data was collected for is no longer served by the retention of personal data and where the retention is no longer necessary for legal or business right.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This obligation seems to complement an individual’s right to withdraw consent in section 16.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, while consumers can withdraw consent of the use, collection and disclosure of their data, with organisations thereafter obligated to cease to do so, this does not squarely extend to the right of consumers to direct organisations to erase their data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The viability of such a provision is, of course, subject to the further perusal of the Ministry, especially with regard to under what circumstances may such a right be circumscribed or exercised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am confident that by passing the Bill, the House would be taking a big step ahead in priming Singapore in our shift to a data-driven economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I thought I might deal with some of them although they are not directly connected with the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Bill which we are debating today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are some matters of confusion, conflation and, perhaps, a misunderstanding, and I hope I can bring some clarity and understanding to the debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That is why, several years ago, when there was a Government data security policy in IM8 and there was not something for the private sector, we enacted the PDPA to improve standards for the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Giam also suggests that, perhaps, we should treat Government and treat businesses the same way, that the same tools and the same behaviours would either be useful or expected in the private realm and the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We expect Government to behave as one service, servicing residents, servicing our citizens, servicing our country as one entity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We expect the private sector to behave as individual entities and there needs to be an appropriate separation and gap in data sharing between private entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have, in Mr Giam's assertions, another confusion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He talked at the beginning of a high compliance burden for public sector officers and then asked later on whether the standards are high enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The high compliance burden is precisely because the standards are high and, perhaps, more burdensome than for the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Nevertheless, there is internal coherence despite the many different Acts and rules and laws that he cited, which are correct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Internally, within the Government, the data security and data privacy space is looked after by the Government Data Office, a single point of contact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is internal coherence, so that we can operate as one Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Members of the public can contact that single point of contact if they are concerned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But if they contact any other arm or organisation within Government, we have our Government working as one through a No Wrong Door policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And that is enabled precisely because there is sharing of data across Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Nevertheless, whoever they contact, they will be referred to the Government Data Office and GovTech to handle the matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is available on the Smart Nation website and it is there for scrutiny and for examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And we can debate and discuss this further if he wishes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Another point of conflation and confusion that I would like to clarify, the monetary fines that are in the PDPA are fines; they are not redress to the individual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They are fines imposed by the regulator on the private sector entity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is no specific provision for compensation to the individual as a result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The individual would need to pursue legal action if they were looking for compensation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Giam suggested that there needed to be some corollary of compensation within the public sector for these fines that the PDPA imposes, should there be a data breach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I just want to be clear that the fines are fines from the regulator and if in the private domain, an individual wishes to pursue compensation, they would have to take legal action in order to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For the Government, there is no special provision or exception or protection for the conduct of the Government or Government officers with respect to data; there is no special carve-out there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The PDPA and the PSGA – the IM8 provisions that Mr Giam referred to – are aligned in terms of standards, the expected behaviour of the officers and entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And they are aligned where there is a single point for people to complain: the PDPC versus the GDSCC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is an option for individuals to pursue mediation and an option for individuals to pursue action for compensation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One of the key other points of confusion I want to address is this idea that the PDPA is equivalent to the PSGA or the Public Sector (Governance) Act, when taken together with a whole series of other laws such as the Official Secrets Act, the Income Tax Act, the Statistics Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These other laws are then on top of the PSGA, governing and controlling behaviour within specific domains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They also apply to the private sector; for example, the Income Tax Act will apply to certain private sector entities as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, the equivalence is between the PSGA and the PDPA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The key issue is then how do we want Government to behave and how do we want our private sector entities to behave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What we want within Government is for sharing of data to achieve that No Wrong Door, One Government responsiveness to citizens, for policy, for execution and implementation as well as for communications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For that, we need to encourage sharing of data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And because Government has roles that do not exist in the private sector, there are additional controls, because of the additional sensitive data that Government has access to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And hence we take this very, very seriously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We prosecute and I give you three examples.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We take this very, very seriously and the public sector officers who handle our data, on behalf of our citizens, know that we take this very, very seriously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The separation of the public and private sector data protection regimes in Singapore remains relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It remains necessary for us to keep achieving the outcomes that we want to achieve in terms of good policy, responsiveness to citizens, operating as One Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It has to be used in a way that drives trust and helps us be effective in maintaining that trust with our citizens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I just want to clarify with the Senior Minister of State that I did not say that the standards for Government should not be higher.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In fact, I agree with the Senior Minister of State that the Government standards should be the same or higher than what it expects of the private sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In fact, I support the No Wrong Door policy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: With regard to data sharing between agencies, I think that is a good thing and it is important for the convenience for our residents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But this provision can also be made within the PDPA, so that Government agencies are allowed to share data between each other.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, why can the myriad of legislation not be brought under the PDPA, so that Singaporeans, public sector officers, will be able to know that there is this harmonised set of data privacy standards that they should all comply with and that they are held to the same standard?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Now, let me first clarify again that I am not saying that currently the Government is operating at a lower standard.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Like I said in my speech, in my experience as a civil servant and my experience working as a government vendor in the past, the standards are very high.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, why can these all not be harmonised under one law, just like how they do it in the GDPR for Europe?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Yes, Senior Minister of State Dr Janil, would you like to respond?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue then is what outcome would he achieve or would we achieve merely by putting it all under one legislation?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I doubt very much there is any confusion among the civil servants about the standards that are expected of them simply because we have two legislative frameworks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue is whether or not the outcomes in terms of the number of data breaches, the security that we have in our systems and the trust that our citizens have in our processes would be assisted by his approach, provided he continues to agree that we are effective at maintaining very high standards within the Government.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The outcomes demonstrate that we are not doing too badly in our public sector.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not have all the numbers but I was looking at their website.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While hacking is not the only type of breach, we can also have, for example, an accidental loss, that is, inadvertent data breaches.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do review them and we can happily get those numbers to Mr Gerald Giam and Members of this House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it demonstrates that our system is not ineffective.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: People know that we have a robust protection regime as he has repeatedly said, that is, our citizens trust us to do the right thing and we must uphold those standards and have these high expectations of our public sector officers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are other jurisdictions in countries, cities and states where they have different legislative frameworks for Government versus the private sector.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue is how you design both of those and whether you make it work for these outcomes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And let me say, categorically, the two are aligned to the same expectations and standards and we will refine them as needed to make sure that that is the case.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, we believe that we need these two approaches because Government is not a private company nor should it behave as such and you cannot expect a private company to behave like Government.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Gerald Giam goes on about the burdens that he felt as a civil servant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If the private SMEs had to comply with all the regulations that he had to struggle with as a civil servant, they would not be able to do business in quite the same way and perhaps innovation and the ease of customer relations, the ease of coming up with new products would be impeded.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there is a difference in behaviour at the entity level and there is a difference of behaviour at an individual level.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, we have to have the right tools to influence behaviour correctly on behalf of our citizens.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That does not mean that we reduce our standards in any way and we have not done so.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I also want to thank them for raising important issues this Bill seeks to address.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I think the comments of Members fall broadly into a few areas about: protecting consumers' personal data, endowing consumers with more control and a greater sense of autonomy and confidence while supporting organisations' legitimate use; and supporting businesses in the use of data for growth and innovation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think in the comments that have been made by Members, it is clear that we all appreciate and recognise that there is an inherent tension between these objectives, and the proposed amendments seek to strike a judicious balance between them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In thinking about these issues and I do propose to address the specific questions raised by Members, it is important that we first recognise that this is a delicate and dynamic balance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is delicate because if we over-correct in one direction, consumers may not retain their confidence and trust in the system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If we swing the other way, then we shackle our businesses and the very benefits that we seek for our consumers and for our economy will diminish.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is dynamic because technology is changing and the ways data is being generated and being put to use are also changing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And therefore, it is imperative that we find our own balance in the way we regulate the collection and use of data in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And there are different jurisdictions with different models.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not think any one of these is universally acclaimed because each has its strengths and its weaknesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is why, in this endeavour of moving this legislative amendment, we have sought to understand the different regimes and to ensure that Singapore is able to remain best-in-class and also ensure that we are nimble and remain interoperable, which is key to our positioning as a node in the international flow of data and digital transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that leads me to the second overall point I want to make, which is we must recognise that whilst legislation and regulation is important, it is not a panacea and neither is it foolproof.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And therefore, what it means is whilst we can put in place rules that will govern the data practices and ensure that data is safeguarded to the best of our ability, we cannot eliminate the risk of data breaches.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is important that we recognise that whilst the rules must be formulated and enforced, it must be complemented by good practices and that has to evolve over time so that we understand, as an overall economic system and as a society, our respective responsibilities and roles.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that brings me to my third overarching point, which is that it is essential that we recognise all of us have a role to play and a responsibility to discharge in maintaining the security and the usability of our data regime and, in a sense, safeguarding the public commons.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, Government formulates the rules and regulations, enforces, provides guidelines and adapts to changing market situations to ensure that we remain abreast, to the best of our ability, of the developments and ensure that we keep Singapore relevant in the context of a new digital economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Businesses must recognise that this is in their self-interest.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not just about complying with rules or regulations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the end of the day, in any competitive domain, businesses will be able to differentiate themselves by their data policy and they will be able to signal the quality of the institution by the kind of approaches they take to safeguard their customers' data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, they must be accountable and responsible, recognising ultimately that it is in their self-interest.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think all of us have the responsibility.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whilst some Members have talked about the so-called power asymmetry, ultimately, I would argue that consumers – individuals like you and me – we are not powerless by any stretch of the imagination.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We can choose to decide whom to do business with or whom to give our custom.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We can choose to decide what data we want to share.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We can choose to decide whether we want to give consent and when we want to withdraw that consent.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, ultimately, we can decide when to sever the relationship if that is what we want.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I think we should not lose sight of that aspect as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ultimately, the legislation must be seen in that perspective.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is one part of an overall architecture that will ensure a vibrant digital economy, but also one where data is respected, it is safeguarded, but also used for appropriate purposes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think it is important to emphasise PDPA recognises organisations' need to use personal data for legitimate purposes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And today, that is accommodated through exceptions to the consent requirement, or as deemed consent.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For all other purposes, organisations have to obtain consent from the individual.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I would like to reinforce this point and a point that Ms Jessica Tan had also picked up, that ultimately, consumers can opt out at any time and they have the freedom to do so.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to assure Mr Desmond Choo that all private sector organisations can rely on these new provisions, regardless of the industry they are in.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And on the whole, the amendments regularise current practices, provide organisations with clarity and confidence to use data, while protecting consumers' interests.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Mr Yip Hon Weng has noted, this will also enhance Singapore's status as an innovation and commercial hub.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some Members have asked about the safeguards for the new provisions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Stricter process safeguards are prescribed for the general legitimate interests exception and deemed consent by notification, while specific exceptions, such as business improvement and research, are tightly scoped.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The safeguards have been designed based on the following principles.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Individuals may withdraw their consent even after the opt-out period.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The PDPC may also require organisations to produce these assessments for its review.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some Members have asked how these provisions might be operationalised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The PDPC has provided guidance on how to conduct risk assessments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will also issue detailed guidance on the legitimate interests exception and how to identify adverse effect, which generally refers to any physical harm, harassment, serious alarm or distress to an individual.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Exceptions for specific purposes, such as business improvement and research purposes, are tightly scoped.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, the business improvement exception supports internal use of data within an organisation or a group of companies, with clearly defined limits.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And when it comes to sending direct marketing messages, organisations still need to obtain express consent.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Sharael Taha enquired about the safeguards for deemed consent by contractual necessity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Essentially, organisations can rely on this provision to share personal data only to the extent necessary to perform their contracts with the individual.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked about the “evaluative purposes".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is actually an existing exception in the PDPA which has now been reclassified under the “legitimate interests exception”.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There has been another set of queries about how we can ensure or have confidence that organisations can be trusted to use personal data in good faith.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I would start by saying firstly, we must recognise, more importantly, organisations must recognise that it is in their self-interest to safeguard personal data as that would foster consumer trust, strengthen their business reputation, and ultimately, their competitiveness and bottom line.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To support that and to ensure organisations take their obligations to protect data seriously, we are introducing both incentives and penalties – carrots and sticks, if you will.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The PDPC will issue new advisory guidelines with examples and illustrations, so that organisations have ample notice of the expected standard of conduct.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As data breaches cannot always be prevented, the PDPC’s enforcement framework reinforces the importance of dealing expeditiously with data breaches to reduce harm, through measures like breach reporting and statutory undertakings.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are also creating market incentives, which can motivate organisations to practise high standards of data protection.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I agree fully with Mr Sharael Taha on the value of certification systems and that is why PDPC launched the Data Protection Trust Mark or DPTM in 2019, to make it easier for consumers to recognise organisations with accountable practices and create the demand for good practices along the entire supply and delivery chain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Organisations with the trust mark require their suppliers and contractors to also adhere to the same standards.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are signs, based on PDPC’s Perception and Awareness Study, that this is having a positive impact on the industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For secure exchanges of personal data with overseas entities, transferring organisations must put in place contractual arrangements or binding corporate rules, to ensure that receiving organisations provide a level of protection comparable to PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Apart from contractual transfer mechanisms, the PDPC joined the APEC Cross Border Privacy Rules, or CBPR, and Privacy Rules for Processors systems.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are multilateral certifications which require participating businesses to implement data protection policies consistent with the APEC Privacy Framework.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Consumers also have a crucial role in safeguarding themselves.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think this is a point that I made earlier, and Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Melvin Yong have reinforced that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why on the part of PDPC, it has reached out to almost 70,000 individuals, including youths, through school talks, exhibitions, community roadshows and events.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am also heartened that these efforts have yielded promising results with consumer awareness of the PDPA and PDPC increasing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Desmond Choo has proposed that a right of erasure be explicitly recognised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I believe Mr Louis Chua was also referring to this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Currently, section 16 of the PDPA provides for individuals to withdraw their consent at any time and the organisation would have to cease the collection, use or disclosure of the personal data unless otherwise required or authorised under any legislation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition, the PDPC can also direct an organisation to destroy personal data collected in contravention of the Act.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whilst they are not identical to the right of erasure, I think they give a substantively similar effect.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On unsolicited messages, Mr Melvin Yong asked about our efforts to address spams and scams.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These actions range from issuing advisory notices and warnings, to prosecution in Court.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The proposed amendments to the PDPA and Spam Control Act establish clear guardrails for sending unsolicited commercial messages, to safeguard consumer interests while permitting legitimate direct marketing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and others have asked about the change in enforcement regime for DNC complaints – why we moved towards a civil administrative regime.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The answer is that the assessment we had is that this would allow for a more efficacious enforcement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Hence, directions and financial penalties are more effective in addressing poor practices by depriving offenders of the financial or commercial gains that they seek.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think it is a more effective way of dealing with this problem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To Ms Joan Pereira’s and Mr Sharael Taha’s queries, our response to spam that originates overseas will continue to be multi-pronged, comprising a mix of public education, industry self-regulation and international collaboration.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Scams, on the other hand – the letter makes all the difference; scams versus spams – scams are serious crimes and they are dealt with by the Police.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are enforced under laws like the Moneylenders Act for unlicensed moneylending; and Penal Code, for example, for cheating offences.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For transnational scams, the Police collaborates closely with foreign law enforcement agencies to investigate and, where possible, cripple these syndicates.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MCI is part of the Inter-Ministry Committee on Scams formed by MHA to combat scam messages and calls.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As many of these scams originate overseas, we have to rely more heavily on technological solutions, as Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Melvin Yong have noted.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Telcos are also blocking international incoming calls that resemble our Government agency or emergency numbers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, these are efforts to help consumers discern and avoid being duped.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I would urge consumers to carefully look at the numbers when they receive calls from overseas because I think this is one way.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We cannot prevent these calls from coming in but we can put up red flags, and this "+" sign and some of these other measures are for that purpose.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will continue to support the Police in their efforts to tackle scams and other illegal activities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There have been questions on compliance costs and higher financial penalties.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think many have asked about what support we are going to give to organisations and clarity for compliance with the new provisions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, these amendments mark the culmination of a multi-year journey.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we would like to ask organisations to see this as part of their own investment and effort in building customer trust and commercial reputation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Instead of conducting selective audits for the few as suggested by Ms Joan Pereira, the PDPC will continue to support organisations by providing guidance, training and access to expertise, and recognising accountable organisations, to inculcate good data protection practices as broadly as possible.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Essentially, we think a comprehensive upstream approach may be more beneficial.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On guidance, PDPC provides accountability tools and resources, such as guides on implementing data protection management programmes, conducting risk assessments and adopting a data protection-by-design approach when developing IT systems.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On training, PDPC has been building up data protection capabilities through the Data Protection Competency Framework and Training Roadmap.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Data Protection Officers or DPOs, trained under this framework will be able to implement robust data protection practices as well as support innovation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On access to expertise, we know and recognise that SMEs may need more help to comply with their data protection obligations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we have developed the Data Protection Starter Kit for them and Data Protection-as-a-Service as an affordable alternative for SMEs to outsource some DPO functions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PDPC also makes simple data protection solutions available on its website for free.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are some concerns about the reasonableness of the increased financial penalty cap.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Desmond Choo proposed aligning the financial penalty cap with other Asian jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The objective here is to ensure that we achieve the requisite deterrent effect on organisations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is why the financial penalties have been calibrated in the way that I have described.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some have asked – I think Mr Patrick Tay was one of them – whether in light of the current circumstances we can exercise some flexibility in how these penalties and other elements are phased in.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we will be informed by the overall circumstances because we are conscious of not wanting to unduly burden our companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The revised penalty cap will apply to breaches that occur after the effective date.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On compliance costs for the Data Portability Obligation, we want to make sure that the approach is balanced and achieves the intended results.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, to address the concerns over the scope of data that can or has to be portable, we have basically intend to help organisations with this new obligation, and introduce the data portability obligation in phases and will issue Regulations and advisory guidelines to provide clarity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we want to make sure we do this in a measured way, clear about where we want to go – our destination – but prepared to be flexible in the path.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On Mr Sharael Taha’s query on the safeguards for individuals, the regulations will prescribe consumer protection measures like cooling-off periods when porting certain types of data, in case consumers change their minds.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To provide additional clarity on scope of implementation, we have also catered for the following: (a) the scope has been narrowed to only cover individuals with whom the porting organisation has an existing and direct relationship; (b) data portability will be scoped to user activity and user provided data in electronic form and will apply only to prescribed categories of data; and (c) organisations are also not required to port data when the burden of porting, including the cost, is unreasonable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the Bill, “significant harm” refers to the impact of a data breach on affected individuals and is used in the context of a data breach notification.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This threshold is based on past enforcement cases and other jurisdictions’ practices as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One example of such data is full name and confidential financial information.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will give more guidance through the Regulations but I want to stress – because I think the question was asked how we derived at these numbers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not think that there is any rocket science or magic behind it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is an exercise in judgement, working with the industry and learning from our experience and past practices to arrive at what we think is a reasonable threshold.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I think what will then have to happen is, we see it in practice and learn from experience, and adapt as we go along.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to assure Mr Louis Ng that PDPC will take a reasonable approach in exercising its powers proportionately and judiciously.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PDPC's decisions are also subject to appeal to the Data Protection Appeal Panel and further appeals can be pursued in the Courts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there is recourse but in the first instance, PDPC will exercise due care and proportionality.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Pereira suggested that organisations notify the PDPC of all data breaches and she also advocated setting a fixed timeframe for notifications to individuals.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Setting such a threshold for notification is important, but we have to take into account the compliance costs on organisations and also focus the effort on potentially systemic issues.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have not set a fixed timeframe for an organisation’s notification to affected individuals of a data breach because data breach circumstances can be very varied.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our positions have been developed in consultation with the public and benchmarked against jurisdictions like Australia, Canada, the EU and California.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I will not rule out anything, but I think in the first instance we want to move forward and see how this works in practice.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There was a question of whether PDPC will exercise its expanded powers appropriately.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The new section 48J details a list of factors that the PDPC will consider before imposing financial penalties.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To Mr Melvin Yong’s query, this will include whether the organisation had previously failed to comply with the PDPA which can be considered as an aggravating factor.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Patrick Tay has raised a very important question on individuals’ mishandling of personal data: how the new offences would apply for mishandling personal data?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We intend for this to apply only to egregious cases.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Employees and service providers who are duly authorised should not have to be concerned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do not intend for these offences to apply in situations where the conduct is solely in the nature of a private dispute.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, a relationship manager transfers his clients’ personal data to his new company with their consent, or a sales agent contacts his clients after commencing new employment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In such cases where the individual reasonably believes that he has the legal right to use or disclose personal data, he has a defence to the new offences.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Such private disputes should continue to be resolved through civil suits or other forms of dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To ensure that these actions are not caught, we have provided for defences under clauses 22 and 38.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Jessica Tan can be assured also that we will further set out in Advisory Guidelines the examples on how the new offences would apply so that organisations and workers have clarity and can continue to use data confidently.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Currently, the exclusion of agents of Government has created a situation where the Government can only hold them to account via contracts or laws such as the Official Secrets Act.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This gap can undermine security as such agents of Government may handle large and sensitive volumes of personal data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: My colleague, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, has explained in detail our approach towards the data regimes in the public and private sectors, so I do not propose to repeat those, but Ms Tin Pei Ling has asked about whether the two regimes would be aligned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We will continue to ensure alignment of data protection principles where the policy intent is the same.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the same vein, the PDPC and the Smart Nation and Digital Government Office or SNDGO are working together to ensure the public sector data protection policies continue to be aligned with the relevant changes to the PDPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I believe I have substantively dealt with the issues that have been raised by Members.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If I may conclude, since the PDPA was enacted eight years ago, we have made significant strides in the extent we use data to make decisions and deliver services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Businesses are employing more sophisticated measures to safeguard personal data.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Consumers are also more aware of the importance of data protection.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We need to adapt to the new landscape where digitalisation has shaped our world, bringing new opportunities but also new risks.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This Bill is an important step in this direction.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It aims to promote strong data governance to enable greater use of data for the benefit of our society and our economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we want is equal emphasis on protection and innovation, so that consumers benefit from data-driven services and solutions, with trust that their data is used responsibly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And businesses use data confidently with proper accountability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And Singapore continues to be an important node in global data flows.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move the amendment* standing in my name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.
